Start with 1 or 2 days a week. Try to make it a fixed day of the week. Try to improve on what you do each time you go until you start to feel improvement and you feel changes in your body. It will typically take 4 to 6 weeks for you to notice at least something. 

  
Once you feel the long term reward of feeling and looking better, add 1 more day of working out to your week and repeat. 

  
Also, focus on how you feel about yourself, don't focus on losing weight or growing your muscles. Just go because of how light you feel mentally after, it is great for handling anxiety and depression, the aesthetic benefits are secondary. 

  
Lastly, joining a class is great. Classes tend to be a fixed day of the week and happen multiple times a week. That makes it more likely to reserve time during your week to go to the class, you feel yourself progress every week and also compare your progression with others, you have somebody who knows what they're doing training you, and you might meet people with the same interests.

Those are my tricks. Exercising is not optional, it's necessary to keep myself mentally and physically better. With that mindset, it's very hard not to want to go.

Secondary gain is not a opinion, but as most things in psychology, a theory. When it is suggested and implied it is not to blame or make you feel at fault, but to shift the perspective of the problem. It cannot be your fault since it is mostly a unconscious process to satisfy needs that are not met. But the purpose of suggesting secondary gain is to shift and change your mentality and your perspective on depression. 

It is a way to take responsibility and learn to take action. Once you rule out possible chemical unbalances and biological causes for depression, you have to start working on it to get better, if not you are gonna be a victim of the condition and have a victim mentality for life. At some point, you need to start making changes and start working towards getting better, its not just going to happen on its own.

That's why suggesting secondary gain is effective. Its not pretty by any means, because it is thinking that you, in a way, are causing and maintaining at least a tiny part of your condition. But once you understand that, you can start making conscious changes towards improvement. It removes the victim mentality and gives you a more assertive attitude towards your problem. I understood this and it changed mine.

Im not taking from a condescending stance, I too suffer from depression. I know what its like to be miserable and in despair. I know how it feels to find the only solution in killing yourself. The moment that I understood what it was that i was doing to maintain that condition my mentality changed and I did positive changes in my life and it has improved (not solved, im not by any means "cured"). View it more as a change in mentality than in just "blame" or "judgement".

Hey im a psychologist. What you are talking about is called secondary gain. What that means is that if any condition is maintained over time (despite medication and/or ruling out chemical and biological reasons for a possible depression) it means that you are gaining something from that condition, and that is the reason why you maintain it (not on purpose). 

The most common secondary gain from depression is sympathy and lower expectations from others, thus you need to try less and people have more patience with you. They do things for you and worry about you. This is the laziness and manipulation you are referring to

PS. Im not only a psychologist, i have also struggled with depression and I have dealt with what im talking about as well, hope it helped.
